result:
Solution 1 is wrong. Its bowtie-free graph does contain bowties. Take the centre u of the star: for two leaves v₁, v₂ and any two distinct y₁, y₂ ∈ Y, the triangles (u, v₁, y₁) and (u, v₂, y₂) share only u. That gives about C(q,2)·b(b−1) bowties, so the claimed zero-bowtie construction fails.

Solutions 2 and 3 both assume that splitting the q added edges between the two parts keeps λ at least λ(K^q). They justify this only with a first-order perturbation estimate, which is the same for both placements when n is even. Their bowtie count (about nq²/8) therefore depends on an unverified spectral inequality. Solution 2's approximations are also cruder, since it uses q/a and q/b shifts without checking the second-order terms.

The bowtie count for K^q itself is ⌊n/2⌋·C(q,2), since each pair of disjoint matching edges in X yields one bowtie at each vertex of Y. I believe the intended answer is ⌊n/2⌋·C(q,2), meaning K^q is extremal. I could not verify that from first principles here. Neither Solution 2 nor Solution 3 gives this value. Solution 3 is the better of the two because its bowtie-counting setup is correct and its exact formula is at least explicit, even though its key spectral step is not justified.

CHOICE: 3
